chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Fazalah, from Al-ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'A man passed by me while I was supplicating in my prayer with my left hand, so he said, "O Abu Abdillah, with your right hand." So I said, "O servant of Allah, for Allah, Blessed and Exalted, is due a right upon this [the left hand] as His right upon this [the right hand]."'

And he (peace be upon him) said: 'Desire (al-rahbah) is that you extend your hands and display their inner parts; and Awe (al-rahabah) is that you extend your hands and display their back parts; and Beseeching (al-tadarru') is that you move the right index finger to the right and left; and Devotion (al-tabattul) is that you move the left index finger, raising it moderately in the sky and lowering it; and Invoking (al-ibtihal) is that you extend your hands and forearms to the sky; and Invoking is when you see the causes for weeping.'

key_terms.التَّبَتُّلُ: Devotion or humility, associated with moving the left index finger moderately.
key_terms.التَّضَرُّعُ: Beseeching or humility, associated with moving the right index finger.
key_terms.الرَّغْبَةُ: Desire or longing, associated with extending hands showing the inner side.
key_terms.الرَّهْبَةُ: Awe or fear, associated with extending hands showing the back side.
key_terms.الِابْتِهَالُ: Invoking or calling out with humility, associated with extending hands and forearms to the sky.

ai.seo_question: What are the different physical gestures for supplication in Shia Islam and what do they signify?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates the nuanced etiquette of supplication by linking specific physical gestures to distinct spiritual states, such as using the inner palms for desire (raghba) and the back of the hands for awe (raghba). This hadith highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the embodiment of inner devotion, where bodily movements like raising the index finger or extending arms serve as tangible expressions of humility and reliance on God. The narration underscores that the manner of raising hands is not merely ritualistic but reflects the supplicant's psychological and spiritual posture before the Divine.
